2. **Install** the DevTools package in your project:
   ```bash
   npm i -D @cnstra/devtools @cnstra/devtools-server @cnstra/devtools-transport-ws
   ```
3. **Configure** your application to connect to DevTools:
   ```ts setup
   import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
   import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
   import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';

   declare const cns: CNS<TCNSNeuron>;
   declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
   ```

   ```ts
   import { CNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools';
   import { CNSDevToolsTransportWs } from '@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws';

   const transport = new CNSDevToolsTransportWs({ 
     url: 'ws://localhost:8080' 
   });
   
   const devtools = new CNSDevTools('my-app', transport, {
     appName: 'My App DevTools',
   });
   
   devtools.registerCNS(cns, registry); // your CNSPersistOptionsRegistry
   ```
4. **Launch** DevTools and start debugging!

## Use Cases

- **Development**: Debug complex neural networks during development
- **Testing**: Verify signal flows and responses in test scenarios
- **Performance**: Identify bottlenecks and optimize neural network performance
- **Production Monitoring**: Monitor live applications (with appropriate security measures)

## Next Steps

- [Download DevTools](/docs/devtools/download) - Get the desktop application
- [Integration Guide](/docs/devtools/integration) - Learn how to integrate DevTools
- [Stimulations](/docs/devtools/stimulations) - The Explorer, Retry and Clone


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/integration

# DevTools Integration

Two ways to run the DevTools UI — pick the one that fits your setup. To mount the
panel inside your own server, behind your own auth, see [Admin](./admin.md).

## Option A: Embedded (one function call)

Best for: Next.js, Vite, any Node.js dev server where you control the process.

```bash
npm i -D @cnstra/devtools-server
```

The examples assume your app keeps its `CNS` in `src/cns.ts`:

```ts file=src/cns.ts
import { CNS, collateral, neuron } from '@cnstra/core';

export const deckCreated = collateral<{ deckId: string }>();
export const cardAdded = collateral<{ deckId: string }>();
export const deckNeuron = neuron({ deckCreated });
export const cardNeuron = neuron({ cardAdded }).dendrite({
    collateral: deckCreated,
    response: (payload, axon) => axon.cardAdded.createSignal(payload),
});
export const cns = new CNS([deckNeuron, cardNeuron]);
```

```ts setup
import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';
import { startCNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';

declare const cns: CNS<TCNSNeuron>;
declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
```

```ts file=dev.ts
// dev.ts  ← excluded from prod entry point
import { startCNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';
import { cns } from './src/cns';
import { registry } from './src/neurons/registry'; // your CNSPersistOptionsRegistry

await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry });
// → 🧠 CNStra DevTools: http://localhost:3141
```

Running a BullMQ or pg-boss worker? Pass the worker itself. It already knows its
`cns`, `registry` and queue; the panel records every job it runs once, under its job id:

```ts
import { createCNSWorker } from '@cnstra/pg-boss';
import type { ICNSPgBossLike } from '@cnstra/pg-boss';

declare const boss: ICNSPgBossLike;

const worker = await createCNSWorker({ boss, cns, registry, queue: 'cns' });
await startCNSDevTools(worker);
```

If you don't have a shared registry yet:

```ts file=src/neurons/registry.ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory } from '@cnstra/persist';
import { deckNeuron, cardNeuron } from '../cns';
export const registry = CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory.create({ deckNeuron, cardNeuron });
```

Opens the browser automatically. The UI, the HTTP endpoints and your CNS instance are all wired up in one call.

### Options

```ts
await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry }, {
    port: 3141,    // default
    open: true,    // auto-open browser (default: true in TTY)
    appId: 'app',  // identifies the SERVICE — the routing key for Retry/Clone
    webSocket: {}, // the panel talks over a WebSocket instead of HTTP polling; loopback only
    consoleLogEnabled: false,
});
```

`appId` is not a display label. It is the key the DevTools server routes commands
by: it keeps `appId → sockets`, and a Retry or Clone is delivered to that set. Run
more than one replica and each one needs its **own** `appId`, or a single Retry
runs on all of them — see
[Running DevTools in a real deployment](./deployments.md).

:::caution Not for a replicated deployment

Given `{ cns, registry }` and no `actions`, Retry and Clone are delivered over the
in-process link to the app, and every replica of the `appId` has its own server.
With more than one replica, pass the worker (a pg-boss worker, or a BullMQ worker
given its `Queue` instance as `queue`) or an `actions` chain so the retry goes through the broker. See
[Retry with replicas](./deployments.md#retry-with-replicas).

:::

### With Next.js

```ts file=next.config.ts
// next.config.ts
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development') {
    const { startCNSDevTools } = await import('@cnstra/devtools-server');
    const { cns } = await import('./src/cns');
    const { registry } = await import('./src/neurons/registry');
    await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry });
}
```

### With Vite

```ts file=vite.config.ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [{
        name: 'cnstra-devtools',
        async buildStart() {
            if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development') {
                const { startCNSDevTools } = await import('@cnstra/devtools-server');
                const { cns } = await import('./src/cns');
                const { registry } = await import('./src/neurons/registry');
                await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry });
            }
        }
    }]
});
```

---

## Option B: Standalone server

Best for: when your app and DevTools server run as separate processes (e.g. browser app, React Native, separate backend).

```bash
# Terminal 1 — start DevTools server
npx @cnstra/devtools-server
# → 🧠 CNStra DevTools: http://localhost:3141

# Or with custom port:
PORT=4000 npx @cnstra/devtools-server
```

The server listens on `127.0.0.1` and answers only requests addressed to that loopback
host, so a web page you open cannot read the runs or send a Retry. Two switches open it up:

- `CNSTRA_DEVTOOLS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173` lets a browser app on another
  origin connect its socket (comma-separated list). A Node or React Native app sends no
  `Origin` and needs nothing.
- `HOST=0.0.0.0` listens on every interface, for a phone or another machine. The Host check
  is then off, and the socket accepts same-origin pages, the allowed origins and clients
  without an `Origin`; there is no authentication, so keep it on a trusted network.

Then connect your app:

```bash
npm i -D @cnstra/devtools @cnstra/devtools-transport-ws
```

```ts
// dev entry point
import { CNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import { CNSDevToolsTransportWs } from '@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws';

const transport = new CNSDevToolsTransportWs({ url: 'ws://localhost:3141' });
const devtools  = new CNSDevTools('my-app', transport, {
    appName: 'My App',
});
devtools.registerCNS(cns, registry); // your CNSPersistOptionsRegistry
```

Open `http://localhost:3141` in your browser.

---

## DevTools Features

Once connected, the Explorer shows every run with its attempts and tasks, per-neuron and per-collateral throughput and errors, and Retry and Clone on a failed run. See [Stimulations](./stimulations.md).

## Production

`startCNSDevTools` is a development server: no auth, its own port. In production,
either leave it out entirely:

- Don't import `@cnstra/devtools-server` or call `startCNSDevTools`
- Don't import `@cnstra/devtools` or `@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws`
- Install every devtools package as a dev dependency (`npm i -D`) only

or mount the panel in your own server behind your own auth, the way an admin
dashboard is mounted — see [Admin](./admin.md).


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/admin

The panel is an admin for your flows: every run, its attempts and tasks, Retry and
Clone. It can run on its own port for development, or be mounted into the server
you already have, under a path, behind the auth you already use.

```ts setup
import type { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from 'http';
import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';
import { createCNSWorker } from '@cnstra/pg-boss';
import type { ICNSPgBossLike } from '@cnstra/pg-boss';
import { createCNSDevToolsHandler, startCNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';

declare const cns: CNS<TCNSNeuron>;
declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
declare const boss: ICNSPgBossLike;
declare function isAdmin(cookie: string | undefined): Promise<boolean>;
declare const middie: unknown;
declare const fastify: {
    register(plugin: unknown): Promise<unknown>;
    use(path: string, handler: (request: IncomingMessage, response: ServerResponse, next: () => void) => void): void;
};
```

## 1. One line

```ts
const worker = await createCNSWorker({ boss, cns, registry, queue: 'cns' });

await startCNSDevTools(worker);
// → 🧠 CNStra DevTools: http://localhost:3141
```

The worker brings its `cns`, its registry and its queue. The panel links to that
`cns` in-process and records every job under its job id, into a bounded in-memory
history (up to 1000 runs) unless you pass a `stimulationRepository`. Retry / Clone
go through pg-boss under the same job id. For BullMQ, pass your `Queue` instance as
`queue` and the worker brings the same link; with only a queue name, Retry and
Clone run in this process, which is fine while there is one. No worker?
Pass `{ cns, registry }`.

This is a development server: its own port, bound to `127.0.0.1` unless you pass
`host`, no auth. Everything below is for running the panel inside your app.

## 2. Mount it in your server

`createCNSDevToolsHandler` takes the same source and options and returns the panel as
a handler, in two shapes: `node` for anything built on Node's `http` (Express,
Connect, Nest, Fastify through middie) and `fetch` for anything built on the Fetch
API (Next.js route handlers, Hono, Bun, Deno). Auth is yours: put your middleware in
front of it, the way you would for any admin route.

### Express

```ts
import express from 'express';

const worker = await createCNSWorker({ boss, cns, registry, queue: 'cns' });
const admin = createCNSDevToolsHandler(worker, { basePath: '/admin/cnstra' });

const app = express();
app.use('/admin/cnstra', async (request, response, next) => {
    if (await isAdmin(request.headers.cookie)) return next();
    response.sendStatus(403);
}, admin.node);
app.listen(3000);
```

`basePath` is the full path the panel lives at. Anything under it that is not the
panel calls `next()`, so your own routes there still work.

### Fastify

Through `@fastify/middie`, which runs before Fastify reads the body:

```ts
const admin = createCNSDevToolsHandler({ cns, registry }, { basePath: '/admin/cnstra' });

await fastify.register(middie);
fastify.use('/admin/cnstra', async (request, response, next) => {
    if (!(await isAdmin(request.headers.cookie))) {
        response.statusCode = 403;
        return response.end();
    }
    return admin.node(request, response, next);
});
```

### Next.js route handler

```ts
// app/admin/cnstra/[[...path]]/route.ts
const admin = createCNSDevToolsHandler({ cns, registry }, { basePath: '/admin/cnstra' });

const handle = async (request: Request): Promise<Response> =>
    (await isAdmin(request.headers.get('cookie') ?? undefined))
        ? admin.fetch(request)
        : new Response('Forbidden', { status: 403 });

export { handle as GET, handle as POST, handle as DELETE };
```

The panel keeps its state in the process: history, the in-process link, open poll
sessions. Run it on the Node.js runtime of a long-lived server (`next start`), not on
an edge or per-request function. A poll waits up to 25 seconds for news; if your
platform cuts requests sooner, lower `polling: { waitMs }` below that limit.

### Hono

```ts
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { basicAuth } from 'hono/basic-auth';

const admin = createCNSDevToolsHandler({ cns, registry }, { basePath: '/admin/cnstra' });

const app = new Hono();
for (const path of ['/admin/cnstra', '/admin/cnstra/*']) {
    app.use(path, basicAuth({ username: 'admin', password: process.env.ADMIN_PASSWORD ?? '' }));
    app.all(path, context => admin.fetch(context.req.raw));
}
```

### Read-only

```ts
const admin = createCNSDevToolsHandler({ cns, registry }, { basePath: '/admin/cnstra', readOnly: true });
```

A read-only panel registers no action links and hides Retry and Clone. The server
answers every Retry, Clone, Launch and command message with a rejection whatever
sends it, so hiding the buttons is not the only thing standing between a viewer and
a rerun.

Whether read-only or not, a browser can only view: polling sessions and WebSocket
clients of the handler are viewers, the server drops any `batch` message they send,
and none of them is ever registered as an app. The only app is the `cns` linked
in-process. A polling `POST` is accepted only with `content-type: application/json`
and answered 415 otherwise, so a page on another site cannot send one without a
CORS preflight, and the handler answers no preflight.

### WebSocket

By default the panel talks to the handler over HTTP polling, which needs nothing
but the routes above. A WebSocket is opt-in, and only with an `authorizeUpgrade` of
your own: an upgrade does not pass through your HTTP middleware, so the handler asks
you directly. Without it no upgrade is accepted.

```ts
import { createServer } from 'http';
import express from 'express';

const admin = createCNSDevToolsHandler({ cns, registry }, {
    basePath: '/admin/cnstra',
    webSocket: { authorizeUpgrade: request => isAdmin(request.headers.cookie) },
});

const app = express();
app.use('/admin/cnstra', admin.node);

const server = createServer(app);
server.on('upgrade', admin.upgrade);
server.listen(3000);
```

`startCNSDevTools` takes the same `webSocket` option. There, leaving out
`authorizeUpgrade` accepts an upgrade only from a loopback address, and only if it
carries no Origin header (a non-browser client) or an Origin equal to the server's own
loopback host and port, so another web page open in the same browser cannot
connect. That default is for the local development server only: behind a proxy
every client arrives from a loopback address, so a deployment passes its own
`authorizeUpgrade`.

### What the handler serves

| path under `basePath` | what |
| --- | --- |
| `/` | the panel page, with its asset URLs pointed at `basePath` and its config embedded |
| `/assets/…` and the other files of the panel build | static files; hashed assets are cached as immutable |
| `/__cnstra/poll` | the polling endpoint of the DevTools protocol |
| `/__cnstra/sync` | the endpoint the panel reads runs, facets and topology from |

No CORS headers are sent: the panel is served from the same origin as its API.
`dispose()` unlinks the panel from the `cns` and closes every session.

### A separate admin process

The handler records runs through its in-process link, so it sees the jobs of the
process it runs in. To run the admin somewhere else, give the workers an `observe`
store they all write to, such as a `CNSPostgresStimulationRepository`, and hand the
same store to the admin as `stimulationRepository`; the admin reads the history from
it. Do not also pass that store to an admin running inside a worker process: the
in-process link already records those jobs, and the store would get each one twice.

## 3. Serve the files yourself

The panel is a static build in `@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/dist`. To serve it from
your own static host on the same origin, copy the folder there, mount the handler at
the same `basePath` for the API routes, and add the config tag the handler would have
added, before the first script of `index.html`:

```html
<script type="application/json" id="cnstra-devtools-config">{"basePath":"/admin/cnstra","transport":"polling","readOnly":false}</script>
```

Serve the page at `/admin/cnstra/`, with the trailing slash, so the build's relative
asset URLs resolve under it.

## 4. A frontend library

To show the panel as a page of the admin you already have, mount the handler as in
section 2 and render the panel from your own frontend, pointed at the same
`basePath`. The panel is shipped as a browser bundle in
`@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/embed`, with its styles in
`@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/embed.css`.

The panel's runtime, Exodra, OIMDB and the CNStra client packages, comes as peer
dependencies, so your app keeps one copy of each:

```bash
npm install @cnstra/devtools-panel-ui @cnstra/core @cnstra/devtools-dto @cnstra/sync @cnstra/oimdb @cnstra/exodra @cnstra/persist-dto @cnstra/types @exodra/core @exodra/dom @exodra/jsx @exodra/context @exodra/list-reconcile @oimdb/core @oimdb/browser @oimdb/exodra
```

### Any frontend

```ts
import { mountCNSDevToolsPanel } from '@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/embed';
import '@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/embed.css';

const element = document.getElementById('cnstra-admin');
const panel = element === null ? undefined : mountCNSDevToolsPanel(element, { url: '/admin/cnstra' });
```

`url` is the base URL of the handler, absolute or relative to the page. `transport`
is `'polling'` by default; pass `'socket'` only to a handler that accepts WebSocket
upgrades. `isReadOnly: true` hides Retry and Clone; refusing them is the handler's
`readOnly`. The panel fills the element's height, so give the element one. Call
`panel.unmount()` when your page leaves the panel: it closes the connection and
removes what it rendered.

If your app already uses OIMDB, pass its database: the panel puts its schema into
your `OIMDB` instead of creating one. This is the recommended way for an app on OIMDB.
Unmounting disposes what the panel created and leaves your database open.

```ts
import { OIMDB } from '@oimdb/core';
import { mountCNSDevToolsPanel } from '@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/embed';

declare const appDb: OIMDB;

const adminElement = document.getElementById('cnstra-admin');
if (adminElement !== null) mountCNSDevToolsPanel(adminElement, { url: '/admin/cnstra', db: appDb });
```

`location` says where the panel keeps its navigation. The default, `'memory'`, keeps
it inside the panel and never touches the page's URL, so your router's hash is safe
and several panels can share a page. With `'hash'`, the way the standalone page
runs, the panel writes the page's URL hash when it connects (the default time window
the server sends) and on every navigation, so it overwrites your hash: mount at most
one such panel per page.

### React

```bash
npm install @cnstra/devtools-panel-react
```

Add it next to the packages above.

```tsx
import { CNSDevToolsPanel } from '@cnstra/devtools-panel-react';
import '@cnstra/devtools-panel-ui/embed.css';

export function AdminCNStraPage() {
    return <CNSDevToolsPanel url="/admin/cnstra" style={{ height: '100vh' }} />;
}
```

`CNSDevToolsPanel` takes the same options as props, `db` included, plus `className` and `style` for
its outer div. It mounts the panel into an inner div of full height, and mounts it
again when `url`, `transport`, `isReadOnly` or `location` change.

### What the panel is

The panel is written in Exodra and renders into its own element, not through React.
Its styles are scoped to that element with `@scope (.cns-devtools)`, so none of them
leak into your admin. The other direction is not sealed: a global rule of your
admin, such as a reset on every button, still reaches the panel's elements.

Compiling the panel's source into plain React components is possible with
`@exodra/to-react`, which translates Exodra machines into React components that
render the same DOM. Its output is complete only when the translator's
`unsupported` list is empty, so check that list for every file. The bundle is the
recommended path.

### Auth

The embed holds no credentials and has no auth of its own: it only calls
`basePath/__cnstra/poll` and `basePath/__cnstra/sync` of the handler, from your
page, with your page's cookies. The handler sends no CORS headers, so `url` must be
on the same origin as the page. Whatever middleware guards those routes in section 2
guards the embedded panel. A WebSocket transport is
authorized by the handler's `authorizeUpgrade`, as in section 2.

## How other admins do it

The shape is the one job-queue dashboards settled on:

- **Bull Board** is mounted on a base path in your Express (or Fastify, Koa, Hono)
  app, and authentication is whatever middleware you put in front of it. Its queue
  adapters take a read-only mode.
- **Sidekiq::Web** is a Rack app you mount in your routes, usually inside a route
  constraint such as Devise's `authenticate` block, so only admins reach it.
- **Hangfire Dashboard** is mounted with an authorization filter, and has a
  read-only switch too.

The panel takes the same shape: a base path, auth by wrapping, read-only as an
option. Unlike Hangfire, the handler has no local-only default for HTTP: mounted in
your server it answers whoever reaches the route, so the auth in front of it is
yours. Only `startCNSDevTools` is local by default: it binds `127.0.0.1`, answers only
requests whose `Host` is this loopback server (a DNS-rebinding page gets 403),
and its WebSocket accepts loopback clients of its own origin.


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/stimulations

The DevTools render the name-based [resumable-execution model](../advanced/resumable-execution.md)
— **Stimulation → Attempt → Task** — in one place: the Explorer.

- **Roster** — every run, newest-first, filterable by status, entry collateral (job type) or
  neuron; keyset-paginated so it stays usable at 20k+ runs.
- **Charts** — a status breakdown and a throughput histogram; `?metric=<path>` in the panel
  URL sums a payload field instead of counting runs.
- **Waterfall** — a selected run's attempts, each neuron-by-neuron task with its in/out
  collaterals and errors — plus **Retry** and **Clone**.

## App side — emit the model

The producer emits the name-based model by default; `trackStimulations` is on unless you
turn it off.

```ts setup
import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';
import type { ICNSDevToolsTransport } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry, ICNSStimulationRepository } from '@cnstra/persist';
import type { TCNSDevToolsActionMiddleware } from '@cnstra/persist-dto';
import { CNSDevToolsServer } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';
import type { ICNSDevToolsServerRepository } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';

declare const DATABASE_URL: string;
declare const transport: ICNSDevToolsTransport;
declare const cns: CNS<TCNSNeuron>;
declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
declare const appTopologyRepo: ICNSDevToolsServerRepository;
declare const repository: ICNSDevToolsServerRepository;
declare const stimulationRepository: ICNSStimulationRepository;
declare const actions: TCNSDevToolsActionMiddleware[];
```

```ts
import { CNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools';

const devtools = new CNSDevTools('my-app', transport, {
  cnsId: 'my-app:core',      // becomes the run's scopeName
  // trackStimulations: true  // default; set false to disable stimulation tracking
});
devtools.registerCNS(cns, registry);
```

Every stimulation on that CNS is streamed as Stimulation/Attempt/Task (the producer runs a
`CNSStimulationPersistor` per run — the same recorder the queue workers use).

## Server side — where the runs are stored

`CNSDevToolsServer` takes the app/topology repository as its first argument and the
**name-based run store** (`ICNSStimulationRepository`) as its second:

```ts
import { CNSPostgresStimulationRepository } from '@cnstra/persist-postgres';

const runStore = new CNSPostgresStimulationRepository({ connectionString: DATABASE_URL });
const server = new CNSDevToolsServer(appTopologyRepo, runStore);
```

Default (omit the 2nd arg) is an in-memory store — great for dev, but
[bound it](../advanced/resumable-execution.md#bound-in-memory) for anything long-running. With
a Postgres store the panel survives restarts and becomes a real admin.

> **Same store as your worker.** Hand that exact `runStore` to a pg-boss / BullMQ worker's
> `observe` and every queue job shows up in the Explorer live — see
> [pg-boss](../integrations/pg-boss.md) / [BullMQ](../integrations/bullmq.md).

## Retry & clone

Select a run to open its waterfall; the two actions are on the header:

- **Retry** — resumes the run's outstanding **frontier** as a new attempt (only the unfinished
  branch re-runs; each task carries its own input signal, so nothing extra is restored). Over the
  wire the server reads the stored `progress`,
  mints attempt *n+1*, and forwards a resume command to the owning app, which hydrates and runs
  `cns.activate(...)`. Rejected if the run has no frontier (nothing to resume).
- **Clone** — a fresh run from the original **entry** (a clean re-do), new id, attempt 1.

### Which one to reach for

They are not two spellings of the same thing, and the difference is what happens to
the record you already have.

**Retry continues the same run.** Same `stimulationId`, one more attempt, and the
run's stored state is updated in place: its `progress` is replaced as the resumed
attempt advances, and its status moves with it. That is what you want when the run
*is* the thing — one job, one order, one id you quote in a ticket — and you simply
need the unfinished part to finish.

**Clone leaves the original alone.** New `stimulationId`, attempt 1, everything
re-runs from the entry signal. Reach for it when the record must not change: an
incident you are still reading, a run you want to compare against, or a fix that
landed in a neuron that already succeeded — Retry would skip that neuron, because
it is not in the frontier any more.

The rule of thumb: **if you would mind losing what the original run recorded, clone
it.**

### Turning one of them off

A server can decide which actions the panel offers, and the panel asks for that on
connect:

```typescript
new CNSDevToolsServer(repository, stimulationRepository, actions, {
    actions: { retry: false },   // this deployment never overwrites a run record
});
```

An action set to `false` is **not drawn** — a greyed-out button reads as "not right
now", which is the wrong story when the answer is "never here". An unset flag means
allowed, so a server that sends no config leaves both buttons exactly as they were.

Typical reasons to use it: a shared staging panel where re-running an order in place
would confuse whoever is reading the incident (turn Retry off), or a deployment
where run ids are business keys and a clone would create one that means nothing
(turn Clone off).

### How far back the panel looks

The Explorer opens on the **last five minutes**. Every screen in it is
time-ordered — the roster, the chart, the facets — and a first query with no
bound makes the store aggregate its whole history to draw one page. On a
development database that is free; on a deployment holding weeks of runs it is
the difference between a panel that opens and one that hangs on connect.

```typescript
new CNSDevToolsServer(repository, stimulationRepository, actions, {
    defaultWindowMs: 60 * 60 * 1000,   // this deployment opens on the last hour
});
```

`0` means the whole history — for a store small enough that the bound only gets
in the way.

It is a **default**, not a filter: it fills the range picker on connect, and the
moment you change the range — or arrive on a link that already carries `since` /
`until` — the panel keeps what it was given and never re-applies the default. A
link to an incident from three days ago shows that incident, not an empty
five-minute window.

The window prunes the store's read before it aggregates, on the same index the
attempts are ordered by, so it costs nothing to widen for one query and go back.

## One-button example

`@cnstra/examples` wires all of this over a real broker + the actual panel:

```bash
npm run demo:panel:bull      # BullMQ (Redis) + the DevTools panel on :8080
npm run demo:panel:pgboss    # pg-boss (Postgres) + the panel
```

Open `http://localhost:8080` → the Explorer shows the broker-backed runs (watch one fail,
**Retry** to resume the frontier, **Clone** for a fresh run). See
[runnable examples](../examples/runnable-examples.md).

## See also

- [Resumable execution](../advanced/resumable-execution.md) — the model, `observe` vs `resume`, stores & bounds.
- [Log correlation](../recipes/log-correlation.md) — tie your logs to the same run ids the panel shows.


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/deployments

Three pods: an Express API that is public, and two replicas of a worker that runs
CNStra. You want the panel. This page is what each id means once there is more than
one process, and what the **Retry** button does when two replicas are connected at
once.

## Where the server runs

The DevTools server is a process of its own. It is **not** something each replica
starts: `startCNSDevTools` boots a server inside your process, which is right for one
dev machine and wrong for a deployment — two replicas would boot two servers,
each seeing only itself.

For a replicated service, run one server and point every replica at it:

```bash
# its own pod / container
npx @cnstra/devtools-server        # listens on 3141
```

```ts setup
import { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry, ICNSStimulationRepository } from '@cnstra/persist';
import type { ICNSDevToolsServerRepository } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';
import { enqueueCNSStimulation } from '@cnstra/bullmq';
import type { ICNSBullActionQueueLike, TCNSStimulationJobData } from '@cnstra/bullmq';

declare const cns: CNS<TCNSNeuron>;
declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
declare const repository: ICNSDevToolsServerRepository;
declare const stimulationRepository: ICNSStimulationRepository;
declare const queue: ICNSBullActionQueueLike;
declare const ordersQueue: ICNSBullActionQueueLike;
declare const job: TCNSStimulationJobData;
declare const order: { id: number };
```

```ts
// in each worker replica — the SAME appId in all of them
import { CNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import { CNSDevToolsTransportWs } from '@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws';

const transport = new CNSDevToolsTransportWs({
    url: process.env.CNSTRA_DEVTOOLS_URL!,   // e.g. ws://cnstra-devtools:3141
});
const devtools = new CNSDevTools('orders-worker', transport, { cnsId: 'orders' });
devtools.registerCNS(cns, registry);
```

The replicas dial **out** to the server, so it needs no route into the pods — an
internal service address is enough, and nothing about DevTools has to be exposed
publicly. Expose only the server's HTTP port, and only to whoever should see your
run data: the panel shows payloads, and anyone who can open it can press Retry.

Keep the server's own storage in mind: it defaults to an in-memory stimulation
store, which dies with the pod. Inject a Postgres store when the run history
should outlive a restart — see [Stimulations](./stimulations.md).

## The three ids

| id | where it comes from | what it identifies | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `appId` | first argument of `new CNSDevTools('orders-worker', transport, …)`, or `startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry }, { appId })` | the **service** — not the process | the routing key: the server keeps `appId → Set<socket>` and delivers a forwarded action to that set |
| `cnsId` | the `cnsId` option; defaults to `` `${appId}:cns` `` | one graph **inside** the service | the topology snapshot is stored under it; one service may host several graphs |
| `scopeName` | recorded on every run — it is the `cnsId` the run executed on | which graph a run belongs to | the server resolves `scopeName → appId` to decide where a resume goes |

**Give each replica its own `appId`** — the pod name, the hostname, anything
unique per process:

```ts
import { CNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import { CNSDevToolsTransportWs } from '@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws';

const transport = new CNSDevToolsTransportWs({ url: process.env.CNSTRA_DEVTOOLS_URL! });
const devtools = new CNSDevTools(
    `orders-worker-${process.env.HOSTNAME}`,
    transport,
);
```

That is what makes a Retry land on **one** pod. The routing chain is
`run.scopeName → findAppByCns → appId → sockets`, and `cnsId` defaults to
`` `${appId}:cns` `` — so a unique `appId` gives each pod a unique `cnsId`, each
run records the `cnsId` it actually executed on, and the retry goes back to
exactly that pod. Share one `appId` across replicas and the last step resolves to
*all* of their sockets, which is how one click becomes N runs (see
[Retry with replicas](#retry-with-replicas)).

:::danger Do not pin `cnsId` to a shared literal while doing this

`cnsId → appId` is a map with last-writer-wins. With unique `appId`s but a
hardcoded `cnsId: 'orders'` in every pod, every run resolves to whichever pod
registered last — the retry runs on the wrong pod, silently. Either let `cnsId`
default, or make it unique too.

:::

What this costs, so you are not surprised:

- **The server keeps one app record per pod**, each with its own copy of the same graph.
- **Dead pods stay.** App records are not removed when a socket
  closes, so across deploys they accumulate; pod names change every rollout.
- **A run whose pod is gone cannot be retried over the socket.** Its `cnsId`
  resolves to an app with no live socket, and the action falls through to the
  next link in the chain — which is another reason to configure a broker link
  when the runs come from a queue.

## The pod with no graph

If the Express pod never constructs a `CNS`, it does not appear in the panel at
all. There is nothing to draw — the panel's unit is a graph, not a process.

If it only enqueues jobs, the run belongs to the **worker's** graph and shows up
there. What ties the two together is the id you choose when you enqueue: with
`jobId` set to a business key, the `stimulationId` in the panel is the same string
your API pod already logged.

```ts
await enqueueCNSStimulation(queue, job, { jobId: `order-${order.id}` });
// panel: stimulationId "order-42", attempts "order-42#1", "order-42#2", …
```

See [Choosing the stimulation id](../integrations/opentelemetry.md#choosing-the-stimulation-id)
for the three ways to pick one and what each costs.

## Topology under a rolling deploy

Every replica pushes its topology snapshot on connect, and snapshots are stored
keyed by `cnsId` — so replicas overwrite each other. While they run identical
code that is harmless: the snapshot they all report is the same one.

During a rolling deploy where the graph itself changed, the panel shows whichever
replica connected last. There is no version or content hash on a snapshot to tell
old from new, and no warning when two differ. Treat the Neurons and Collaterals diagrams as unreliable
for the duration of a rollout of a changed topology; the run data (Stimulation →
Attempt → Task) is unaffected, because each run carries its own names.

## Retry with replicas

Panel actions — Retry, Clone — go through an ordered middleware chain, the third
constructor argument of `CNSDevToolsServer`. The server appends its own link
**last**: forward the action to the app over its socket.

That socket link sends to **every** connected socket of the app. If replicas
share one `appId`, one Retry click runs the resumed frontier on **all** of them —
nothing de-duplicates it. Giving each replica its own `appId` (see
[The three ids](#the-three-ids)) is what keeps that set down to the single pod
that ran the job.

In production, put a broker link in front so the retry goes through the queue,
where delivery and de-duplication are the broker's problem:

```typescript
import { CNSDevToolsServer } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';
import { createCNSBullActions } from '@cnstra/bullmq';

new CNSDevToolsServer(repository, stimulationRepository, [
    createCNSBullActions(ordersQueue),
]);
```

`createCNSBullActions` asks the queue whether it holds a job with that
`stimulationId`:

- **yes** → it calls the broker's own `job.retry()`. Same job id, history kept,
  `attemptsMade` incremented, and the resume checkpoint is found by that same id —
  so the frontier does not have to be shipped anywhere. The link stops the chain.
- **no** → the run did not come from this queue, so the link calls `next()` and
  the action carries on down the chain.

`createCNSPgBossActions(boss, queue)` is the pg-boss equivalent, same shape and same
reasoning. A Clone or Replay is a new run, so both links enqueue a new job under
the new id instead.

Runs that were started by an HTTP handler or a cron rather than by the queue fall
through the broker link and reach the socket link — which is what an in-process
CNS needs. So a mixed deployment works, with the replica caveat above applying
only to the runs that reach the socket link.

If the chain runs out with nobody acting, the panel is told the action was
rejected (`no runtime accepted the retry`) rather than being left with a button
that reported success and did nothing.

`startCNSDevTools` and `createCNSDevToolsHandler` take the same `actions` and `ui`
options and pass them to the server they build; a pg-boss worker, or a BullMQ
worker given its `Queue` instance as `queue`, passed as the source brings its own link. An in-process panel does not have
to be reassembled by hand to route Retry through a broker — see [Admin](./admin.md).

## When the network will not carry a WebSocket

A standalone server is reached over whatever sits in front of it, and that is the
one deployment where the panel's default connection can fail outright: an ingress
with upgrades off, a corporate proxy, a platform that cuts long-lived connections.
The panel then reconnects forever and shows nothing, while the server is healthy.

Both sides can fall back to HTTP, on the same port, at `/__cnstra/poll` — always
exposed, no flag to turn it on. The socket stays the default; polling is what a
client asks for. On polling the panel reads its lists and details with one
`GET /__cnstra/sync` per poll and sends Retry, Clone and the queue commands
through `/__cnstra/poll`, so an ingress in front of it lets both paths through.

- **The panel** — open it with `?transport=polling`. That is a link you can hand
  to whoever is behind the proxy without changing anything for everyone else, and
  the header reads `· polling` so nobody wonders why the view is a poll behind.
- **An app** — swap `@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws` for
  `@cnstra/devtools-transport-http`; the constructor takes the same `url`, over
  `http://` rather than `ws://`.

Sessions are held by id and dropped after a minute of silence — a polling client
has no `close` event, so going quiet is the only signal it gives. That is also
what takes it out of Retry routing, which matters here: a session kept forever
would keep being offered actions it will never carry out. Both timings are on
`polling` (`waitMs`, `sessionTtlMs`); the defaults park a poll for 25s, under the
read timeout of the proxies that make polling necessary in the first place.

## See also

- [Middleware chains](../advanced/middleware.md) — writing your own action link, and the separate write chain
- [Stimulations (Explorer)](./stimulations.md) — what Retry and Clone do to the run model
- [Integration](./integration.md) — the two ways to run the panel


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/frameworks

The panel does not care what serves your HTTP. It needs two things — the `CNS`
instance and the registry that names its neurons — and one decision: does the
DevTools server run inside your process, or beside it.

- **Inside your process** (`startCNSDevTools`) — one call, no extra deployment. Right
  for local development and a single-process app.
- **Beside it** (a standalone `@cnstra/devtools-server`, apps dial out to it) — the
  only option once you run more than one replica, because an in-process server
  would exist once per replica and each would see only itself. See
  [Deployments](./deployments.md).

Everything below is the first shape. The second is the same in every framework:
construct `CNSDevTools` with a WebSocket transport where you would have called
`startCNSDevTools`.

The examples assume an app with these two modules:

```ts file=src/cns.ts
import { CNS, collateral, neuron } from '@cnstra/core';

export type TOrder = { id: string };
export const orderCreated = collateral<TOrder>();
export const orderAccepted = collateral<TOrder>();
export const orders = neuron({ orderAccepted }).dendrite({
    collateral: orderCreated,
    response: (order, axon) => axon.orderAccepted.createSignal(order),
});
export const cns = new CNS([orders]);
export type TOrdersCNS = typeof cns;
```

```ts file=src/neurons/registry.ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory } from '@cnstra/persist';
import { orders } from '../cns';

export const registry = CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory.create({ orders });
```

```ts setup
import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
import type { ICNSBullActionQueueLike } from '@cnstra/bullmq';
import { startCNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';
import { CNSDevTools } from '@cnstra/devtools';

declare const cns: CNS<TCNSNeuron>;
declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
declare const ordersQueue: ICNSBullActionQueueLike;
declare function Fastify(): { listen(options: { port: number }): Promise<string> };
```

## Plain Express

Keep the call out of the module that defines your routes, so nothing about
DevTools is reachable from the request path:

```ts file=src/server.ts
// src/server.ts
import express from 'express';
import { cns, orderCreated } from './cns';
import { registry } from './neurons/registry';

const app = express();
app.post('/orders', async (req, res) => {
    await cns.stimulate(orderCreated.createSignal(req.body)).waitUntilComplete();
    res.sendStatus(202);
});

const server = app.listen(3000);

// DevTools is a development tool: it shows payloads and offers Retry to anyone
// who can open it. Gate it, do not ship it on by accident.
if (process.env.CNSTRA_DEVTOOLS === '1') {
    const { startCNSDevTools } = await import('@cnstra/devtools-server');
    const devtools = await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry }, {
        appId: 'orders-api',
    });
    console.log(`DevTools: ${devtools.url}`);

    process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
        devtools.stop();
        server.close();
    });
}
```

Two details worth knowing:

- **`open`** defaults to whether stdout is a TTY, so a container already gets
  `false` and a local `npm run dev` gets `true`. Set it explicitly only when you
  want the opposite of that.
- **The dynamic `import`** is the point of the flag. With a static import the
  package sits in your production bundle and its dependencies are installed in
  production, even when the flag is off.

## NestJS

Nest owns the lifecycle, so the panel goes in a module that starts it on init and
stops it on shutdown. The `CNS` and the registry become ordinary providers:

```ts file=src/cns.module.ts
// cns.module.ts
import { Module, Inject } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { TCNSDevToolsHandle } from '@cnstra/devtools-server';
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
import { cns, type TOrdersCNS } from './cns';
import { registry } from './neurons/registry';

export const CNS = Symbol('CNS');
export const REGISTRY = Symbol('CNS_REGISTRY');

@Module({
    providers: [
        { provide: CNS, useValue: cns },
        { provide: REGISTRY, useValue: registry },
    ],
    exports: [CNS, REGISTRY],
})
export class CnsModule {
    private devtools?: TCNSDevToolsHandle;

    constructor(
        @Inject(CNS) private readonly cns: TOrdersCNS,
        @Inject(REGISTRY) private readonly registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry,
    ) {}

    async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
        if (process.env.CNSTRA_DEVTOOLS !== '1') return;
        const { startCNSDevTools } = await import('@cnstra/devtools-server');
        this.devtools = await startCNSDevTools({ cns: this.cns, registry: this.registry }, {
            appId: 'orders-api',
        });
    }

    onApplicationShutdown(): void {
        this.devtools?.stop();
    }
}
```

`onApplicationShutdown` only fires if you called `app.enableShutdownHooks()` —
without it the panel's port stays held until the process is killed, which is
exactly the kind of thing that makes a redeploy hang.

Inject `CNS` wherever you stimulate:

```ts file=src/orders.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { orderCreated, type TOrder, type TOrdersCNS } from './cns';
import { CNS } from './cns.module';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
    constructor(@Inject(CNS) private readonly cns: TOrdersCNS) {}

    async create(order: TOrder): Promise<void> {
        await this.cns
            .stimulate(orderCreated.createSignal(order))
            .waitUntilComplete();
    }
}
```

## Fastify, Koa, anything else

Identical to Express — the panel runs its own HTTP listener on its own port and
shares nothing with yours:

```ts
const fastify = Fastify();
await fastify.listen({ port: 3000 });

if (process.env.CNSTRA_DEVTOOLS === '1') {
    const { startCNSDevTools } = await import('@cnstra/devtools-server');
    await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry }, { appId: 'orders-api' });
}
```

Nothing about DevTools sits on your request path, so it cannot slow a route down or
leak into a response. To serve the panel from your own server instead, under a path
and behind your auth, see [Admin](./admin.md).

## Keeping run history across restarts

By default the panel's store is in-memory and dies with the process — fine for
development, useless the moment you restart while reading an incident. Pass a
Postgres store. The panel records every run of this process into it, jobs and
HTTP-triggered runs alike, so a worker in the same process needs no `observe` of
its own; an admin in another process reads the `observe` store the workers write to:

```ts
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import { CNSPostgresStimulationRepository, CNSPostgresStimulationSchema } from '@cnstra/persist-postgres';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
await CNSPostgresStimulationSchema.migrate(pool);   // once, from a place you control
const runs = new CNSPostgresStimulationRepository({ pool });

await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry }, { stimulationRepository: runs });
```

See [Stimulations](./stimulations.md) for what the store holds and
[Deployments](./deployments.md) for running the server separately.

## Retry through a queue, and hiding an action

`startCNSDevTools` takes the same knobs as the server it builds, so you do not
have to drop to assembling one by hand as soon as you need them:

```ts
import { createCNSBullActions } from '@cnstra/bullmq';

await startCNSDevTools({ cns, registry }, {
    appId: 'orders-api',
    // Retry goes through BullMQ instead of the in-process link — which is what
    // stops one click running on every replica.
    actions: [createCNSBullActions(ordersQueue)],
    // This deployment never overwrites a run's record in place.
    ui: { actions: { retry: false } },
});
```

A worker passed as the first argument brings its own link instead: a pg-boss
worker always, a BullMQ worker when its `queue` is a `Queue` instance rather than a name.

Both are explained in [Deployments](./deployments.md#retry-with-replicas) and
[Retry & clone](./stimulations.md#retry--clone).

## What the panel needs from your network

**For a standalone server, a WebSocket in both directions by default.** The panel
opens a `WebSocket` to the server, and the app connects with
`@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws`. All protocol traffic is on the socket; the HTTP
port otherwise serves the panel's assets. `startCNSDevTools` is the other way
round: the app is linked in-process, and the panel polls over HTTP unless you pass
`webSocket`.

That matters when something between you and the server does not pass WebSocket
upgrades. Typical culprits: an ingress or load balancer with upgrades off, a
corporate proxy, a serverless platform that terminates long-lived connections.
Without a fallback the panel would sit reconnecting and show nothing.

**There is an HTTP fallback for both sides.** The server always exposes it at
`/__cnstra/poll` on the same port; the socket stays the default and polling is
what you switch to when an upgrade will not get through.

For the panel, add `?transport=polling` to its URL — that is a link you can hand
to whoever is stuck behind the proxy, and the header shows `· polling` so nobody
wonders why the view is a poll behind.

For the app, swap the transport:

```ts
import { CNSDevToolsTransportHttp } from '@cnstra/devtools-transport-http';

const transport = new CNSDevToolsTransportHttp({ url: 'http://cnstra-devtools:3141' });
const devtools = new CNSDevTools('orders-worker', transport);
```

Both sides speak the same protocol over three endpoints — a `POST` per message, a
long `GET` that parks until something is queued, a `DELETE` on shutdown. Expect
the panel to lag by up to one poll, and a failed request to back off rather than
retry tightly.

## Before you turn it on outside development

- The panel **shows payloads**. Whatever your signals carry — a customer address,
  a token — is visible to anyone who can open it. Redact at the write path if that
  matters: [Middleware chains](../advanced/middleware.md).
- The panel **offers Retry and Clone**. Both re-run real work. A server can turn
  either off — see [Retry & clone](./stimulations.md#retry--clone).
- Bind it to an internal address. Nothing in DevTools authenticates anybody.


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/mcp

`@cnstra/mcp` is an MCP server that gives AI tools (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf) live access to your neuron graph. It uses the same registry you create with `CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory` from `@cnstra/persist` — one file, one line.

Tools exposed:
- **`cns_get_context`** — START HERE: CNStra concept guide + neuron list
- **`cns_get_graph`** — full architecture with all connections
- **`cns_get_neuron`** — deep dive into one neuron
- **`cns_list_neurons`** — quick overview of all neurons
- **`cns_list_collaterals`** — all collaterals with owners and subscribers

## Setup

### 1. Install

```bash
npm i -D @cnstra/mcp
```

### 2. Create cns-mcp.ts

The examples assume your neurons live in `src/neurons/index.ts` and the `CNS` in `src/cns.ts`:

```ts file=src/neurons/index.ts
import { collateral, neuron } from '@cnstra/core';

export const userLogin = collateral<{ userId: string }>();
export const deckCreated = collateral<{ deckId: string }>();
export const cardAdded = collateral<{ deckId: string }>();
export const deckNeuron = neuron({ deckCreated }).dendrite({
    collateral: userLogin,
    response: ({ userId }, axon) => axon.deckCreated.createSignal({ deckId: userId }),
});
export const cardNeuron = neuron({ cardAdded }).dendrite({
    collateral: deckCreated,
    response: (payload, axon) => axon.cardAdded.createSignal(payload),
});
export const uiNeuron = neuron({});
```

```ts file=src/cns.ts
import { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import { deckNeuron, cardNeuron, uiNeuron } from './neurons/index';

export const cns = new CNS([deckNeuron, cardNeuron, uiNeuron]);
```

First, create a registry. Two options:

**Option A — per-file (recommended for larger projects):**
```ts file=src/neurons/registry.ts
// src/neurons/registry.ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
export const registry = new CNSPersistOptionsRegistry();
```

```ts file=src/neurons/deck.ts
// src/neurons/deck.ts — each neuron registers itself
import { registry } from './registry';
import { deckNeuron, cardNeuron, userLogin } from './index';

registry
    .register('deckNeuron', deckNeuron, { deckCreated: 'deck-created' }) // explicit collateral names
    .register('cardNeuron', cardNeuron)
    .registerCollateral('userLogin', userLogin); // standalone collateral (no neuron owner)
```

**Option B — all at once (simpler for small projects):**
```ts file=src/neurons/registry-all-at-once.ts
// src/neurons/registry.ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory } from '@cnstra/persist';
import { deckNeuron, cardNeuron, uiNeuron } from './index';

export const registry = CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory.create({ deckNeuron, cardNeuron, uiNeuron });
```

Then the MCP entry point:

```ts file=cns-mcp.ts
// cns-mcp.ts  ← dev-only, not imported from prod entry point
import { startCNSMCPServer } from '@cnstra/mcp';
import { cns } from './src/cns';
import { registry } from './src/neurons/registry';

await startCNSMCPServer(cns, registry);
```

### 3. Run init to register with all AI tools

```bash
npx @cnstra/mcp init
```

Writes MCP config for every tool found in the project:

| Tool | Config file |
|------|-------------|
| Claude Code | `.claude/settings.json` → `mcpServers` |
| Cursor | `.cursor/mcp.json` → `mcpServers` |
| VS Code | `.vscode/mcp.json` → `servers` |
| Windsurf | `.windsurf/mcp.json` → `mcpServers` |

After `init`, open the project in any of these tools — the MCP server starts automatically.

## What the AI gets

The server exposes three MCP mechanisms — tools that support any subset will benefit:

**Resources** (auto-loaded on connect in tools that support them):
- `cnstra://context` — concepts, rules, neuron list
- `cnstra://graph` — full neuron graph

**Prompts** (slash-commands / @ references):
- `understand_project` — context + full graph in one shot

**Tools** (called on demand):
- `cns_get_context`, `cns_get_graph`, `cns_get_neuron`, `cns_list_neurons`, `cns_list_collaterals`

### Example: cns_get_graph output

```markdown
# CNS Graph

## deckNeuron

**Emits:**
  - `createdAtButtonClick` → cardNeuron
  - `createdAtOnboarding` → cardNeuron
  - `renamed`
  - `archived`

**Reacts to:**
  - `createDeckButtonClicked` from **uiNeuron**
  - `userOnboarded` from **onboardingNeuron**
```

## Zero prod overhead

`@cnstra/mcp` is a dev dependency. `cns-mcp.ts` is never imported in production. The MCP server process only runs when an AI tool starts it.


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/ai-inspection

AI tools like Claude and Cursor understand your CNStra application much better when they can read the neuron graph and runtime history as plain text — instead of parsing dozens of source files.

`@cnstra/devtools` exports two utilities for this: `dumpCNSGraph` and `CNSHistoryLogger`. Both take a registry created with `CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory` — one line, no boilerplate.

## Static graph dump

`dumpCNSGraph` produces a Markdown description of your neuron graph: which collaterals each neuron emits, where those collaterals go, and what each neuron reacts to.

```ts file=cns.ts setup
import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
export declare const cns: CNS<any>;
```

```ts file=neurons.ts setup
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';
export declare const deckNeuron: TCNSNeuron<any>;
export declare const cardNeuron: TCNSNeuron<any>;
```

```ts file=src/neurons/registry.ts setup
import type { CNSPersistOptionsRegistry } from '@cnstra/persist';
export declare const registry: CNSPersistOptionsRegistry;
```

```ts file=cns.debug.ts
// cns.debug.ts  ← excluded from your prod entry point
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';
import { dumpCNSGraph } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import { cns } from './cns';
import { registry } from './src/neurons/registry'; // your CNSPersistOptionsRegistry

writeFileSync('CNS_GRAPH.md', dumpCNSGraph(cns, registry));
```

If you don't have a shared registry yet, create one inline:

```ts setup
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';
import { dumpCNSGraph, CNSHistoryLogger } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import type { CNS } from '@cnstra/core';
import type { TCNSNeuron } from '@cnstra/types';

declare const cns: CNS<any>;
declare const deckNeuron: TCNSNeuron<any>;
declare const cardNeuron: TCNSNeuron<any>;
declare const uiNeuron: TCNSNeuron<any>;
```

```ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory } from '@cnstra/persist';
const registry = CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory.create({ deckNeuron, cardNeuron, uiNeuron });
writeFileSync('CNS_GRAPH.md', dumpCNSGraph(cns, registry));
```

Add a script to `package.json`:

```json
{ "scripts": { "graph": "tsx cns.debug.ts" } }
```

Run `npm run graph` whenever your neuron structure changes. Commit `CNS_GRAPH.md` — AI tools will pick it up automatically.

### Example output

```markdown
# CNS Graph

## deckNeuron

**Emits:**
  - `createdAtButtonClick` → cardNeuron
  - `createdAtOnboarding` → cardNeuron
  - `renamed`
  - `archived`

**Reacts to:**
  - `createDeckButtonClicked` from **uiNeuron**
  - `userOnboarded` from **onboardingNeuron**
```

## Runtime history

`CNSHistoryLogger` subscribes to a CNS instance and records the stimulation history.

```ts file=history.debug.ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory } from '@cnstra/persist';
import { CNSHistoryLogger } from '@cnstra/devtools';
import { cns } from './cns';
import { deckNeuron, cardNeuron } from './neurons';

const registry = CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory.create({ deckNeuron, cardNeuron });

const logger = new CNSHistoryLogger(cns, registry);

// ... run your app, trigger some flows ...

console.log(logger.dump());
// or: writeFileSync('CNS_HISTORY.md', logger.dump());

logger.stop();
```

### Options

```ts
import { CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory } from '@cnstra/persist';

new CNSHistoryLogger(cns, CNSPersistOptionsRegistryFactory.create({ deckNeuron, cardNeuron }), {
    maxRecords: 50, // keep last N stimulations (default: 100)
});
```

### Example output

```markdown
# CNS History

### #3 · 12:00:05.234
triggered by: `userOnboarded`
  - `userOnboarded` → `createdAtOnboarding`
  - `createdAtOnboarding` → `createdAtOnboarding`

### #2 · 12:00:02.100
triggered by: `createDeckButtonClicked`
  - `createDeckButtonClicked` → `createdAtButtonClick`
```

## Zero prod overhead

Both utilities are in `@cnstra/devtools` (dev dependency). As long as `cns.debug.ts` is not in your production entry point, they are fully tree-shaken.

For live AI access to the graph without generating files, see the [MCP Server](/docs/devtools/mcp).


# Source: https://cnstra.org/docs/devtools/download

# Download CNStra DevTools

Desktop application for debugging and monitoring CNStra applications.

## Features

- **Server Manager**: Start/stop DevTools servers on custom ports
- **Live Monitoring**: Real-time view of runs, their tasks, and per-neuron throughput and errors
- **Cross-Platform**: Available for macOS, Windows, and Linux

## Installation

import BrowserOnly from '@docusaurus/BrowserOnly';

<BrowserOnly>
  {() => {
    const React = require('react');
    const [state, setState] = React.useState({ loading: true, url: '', error: '' });

    React.useEffect(() => {
      async function pick() {
        try {
          const platform = (window.navigator.platform || '').toLowerCase();
          const ua = (window.navigator.userAgent || '').toLowerCase();
          const isMac = platform.includes('mac') || ua.includes('mac');
          const isWindows = platform.includes('win') || ua.includes('win');
          const isLinux = (platform.includes('linux') || ua.includes('linux')) && !ua.includes('android');
          const isArm = ua.includes('arm') || ua.includes('aarch64') || ua.includes('apple');

          const res = await fetch('https://api.github.com/repos/abaikov/cnstra/releases/latest', { headers: { 'Accept': 'application/vnd.github+json' } });
          if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Failed to fetch latest release');
          const json = await res.json();
          const assets = json.assets || [];

          function findAsset(regex) {
            return assets.find(a => regex.test(a.name));
          }

          let asset;
          if (isMac) {
            // Prefer DMG; choose arch by UA
            asset = isArm
              ? findAsset(/DevTools-.*-arm64\.dmg$/)
              : findAsset(/DevTools-.*-x64\.dmg$/) || findAsset(/DevTools-.*-intel\.dmg$/);
          } else if (isWindows) {
            asset = findAsset(/Setup .*\.exe$/) || findAsset(/DevTools-.*\.exe$/);
          } else if (isLinux) {
            asset = findAsset(/DevTools-.*\.AppImage$/);
          }

          if (!asset) throw new Error('No matching asset for your platform');
          setState({ loading: false, url: asset.browser_download_url, error: '' });
        } catch (e) {
          setState({ loading: false, url: '', error: (e && e.message) || 'Unknown error' });
        }
      }
      pick();
    }, []);

    return (
      <div>
        {state.loading ? (
          <p>Detecting your platform and preparing the latest download…</p>
        ) : state.url ? (
          <div>
            <a className="button button--primary button--lg" href={state.url}>Download latest for your system</a>
            <p style={{ marginTop: 8 }}>
              Not your platform? <a href="https://github.com/abaikov/cnstra/releases/latest">See all downloads</a>
            </p>
          </div>
        ) : (
          <div>
            <p>Could not determine a suitable installer automatically.</p>
            <p><a href="https://github.com/abaikov/cnstra/releases/latest">Open latest releases page</a> and pick your platform manually.</p>
            {state.error && <pre>{state.error}</pre>}
          </div>
        )}
      </div>
    );
  }}
</BrowserOnly>

## Usage

1. Launch CNStra DevTools
2. Click "Start Server" to spawn a DevTools server (default port: 8080)
3. In your application, configure DevTools transport:

```typescript
import { CNSDevToolsTransportWs } from '@cnstra/devtools-transport-ws';

const transport = new CNSDevToolsTransportWs({
  url: 'ws://localhost:8080'
});
```

4. Click "Open Panel" in the manager to view your application's neural network

## All Releases

View all versions and release notes on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/abaikov/cnstra/releases).
